figures.attributes: #fig-master-loop fig-alt="Context and information lead into notice and interpret; construct options; predict consequences; value consequences; choose and commit; and observe and learn. One shared green return path branches into the five decision functions before observation and learning. It has no direct arrow to the current inputs. An enclosing frame shows that people, institutions, and design can shape the whole process. The map organizes questions rather than specifying a fixed psychological sequence." .phone-fit

#fig-normative-decision-loop fig-alt="A normative decision loop. Information about alternatives enters a judgment box containing prediction followed by valuation. Valuation supports choice, choice leads to an outcome, and feedback from the outcome can inform later judgment."

#fig-behavioral-decision-loop fig-alt="A behavioral decision loop. External context shapes presented information and the decision-maker's internal state and model. Within judgment, selection and interpretation have two-way connections with prediction and valuation. Judgment supports choice and action, choice leads to an outcome, and feedback may update the internal model."

#fig-laptop-distraction .phone-fit fig-alt="Two separate experiments compare average comprehension scores. In the first, laptop note takers scored 66 percent without additional online tasks and 55 percent with them. In the second, paper note takers scored 73 percent without a view of multitasking laptops and 56 percent with a view. Error bars show standard errors."

#fig-attention-filter fig-alt="Many information streams compete for selection. Goals, salience, expectations, and load influence which signals become consciously reportable and deliberately usable. Unselected information may still receive limited processing."

#fig-sensory-windows fig-alt="Four pencil-style scenes show a pit viper sensing infrared radiation from a warm mouse with its facial pit; a bee beside matched flowers in visible light and false-colour ultraviolet, revealing a dark petal-base pattern; Asian elephants with low-frequency sound waves; and a European robin beside schematic geomagnetic field lines." .wide-illustration

#fig-recognition-two-tone fig-alt="Irregular black patches on a white field. Some form small isolated clusters, while others join into larger dark regions. The image's subject is deliberately left unnamed for this recognition exercise." width=100% .phone-fit

#fig-context-b13-demonstration fig-alt="Two horizontal rows contain the same central ambiguous mark. The top row places it between 12 and 14, encouraging a reading of 13. The bottom row places it between A and C, encouraging a reading of B." width=100%

#fig-duck-rabbit-context fig-alt="A single navy outline on white has a shared eye, rounded head, and two long extensions pointing right. It can be interpreted as a duck facing right, with the extensions forming its bill, or as a rabbit facing left, with the extensions forming its ears." width=100% .phone-fit

#fig-perception-context-lab fig-alt="Three panels compare physically identical targets in different contexts. Equal horizontal shafts have different arrow fins, equal blue centre circles are surrounded by small or large circles, and identical grey patches appear on dark and light backgrounds. Each panel states the physical equality." width=100%

#fig-traffic-light-color-context fig-alt="The left panel contains only a gray textured lens on a plain blue-green background, with no frame or other objects. The right places the identical lens at the same size and height at the top of a three-lamp traffic signal in a blue-green scene. The familiar upper position supplies the learned expectation of red." width=100% .phone-fit

#fig-predictive-processing-decision fig-alt="Expectations and incoming signals converge on perception. Perception informs action and sampling, which changes the next evidence. A feedback arrow shows that mismatch can update the internal model."

#fig-recognition-grayscale fig-alt="A grayscale illustration of a Dalmatian resting in dappled shade, its head facing left. Its nose is near the center-left, its eye is above it, and a dark ear hangs on the right." width=100% .phone-fit

#fig-expectation-loop fig-alt="An expectation branches into four parallel pathways: physiological response, behavior and effort, other people's responses, and resources and opportunities. The pathways converge on changed outcomes and evidence. A feedback path distinguishes self-fulfilling reinforcement from self-defeating prevention."

#fig-valuation fig-alt="Four groups of possible influences converge on current value: the option and comparisons, current state, goals and experience, and social meaning. Current value can guide motivation and choice."

#fig-overlapping-motive-systems fig-alt="A pile of seven complete, overlapping triangles shows proposed motive systems. From the broadest triangle upward, they are immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, status and esteem, mate acquisition, mate retention, and kin care. The exposed diagonal edges show that later-developing systems are added without removing earlier systems. A developmental guide labels the direction from earlier to later emergence."

#fig-choice-blindness-swap fig-alt="A three-stage sequence uses striped and dotted abstract cards. The chooser selects the striped card, the cards are covertly swapped during handling, and the dotted card is then presented with the question why did you choose this one." width=100%
#fig-narrator-learning fig-alt="Choice leads to outcome, narrative, and a future rule, while a contemporaneous decision record provides an independent comparison for detecting hindsight."
#fig-heuristic-substitution fig-alt="A target question is replaced by an easier question and then produces a quick answer." .phone-fit

#fig-fast-slow fig-alt="Two columns summarize System 1 and System 2 processing features. System 1 is typically fast, automatic, low effort, associative, and cue driven. System 2 is typically working-memory dependent, effortful, rule guided, and capable of hypothetical reasoning. Arrows show candidate answers and possible inspection or training." .phone-fit
#fig-daughter-finger-counting fig-alt="A three-year-old child looks down at her hands while counting on her fingers to work out four plus one." width=42% fig-align="center"

#fig-stroop-interference-lab fig-alt="Two large rows ask the reader to name ink colour. The neutral row contains red, blue, green, and orange strings of X characters. The conflict row contains colour words printed in incongruent colours." width=100%

#fig-affect-panda-sea-star fig-alt="A fluffy giant panda cub rests its tilted head against a tree fork and hugs the branch. Beside it, purple and orange ochre sea stars with thick, textured arms cling to wet intertidal rocks among mussels and algae. Both scenes receive equal visual space; the illustration provides no evidence about their relative conservation value." width="88%"
#fig-affect-availability fig-alt="Affect and available examples converge on a substituted judgment, followed by a denominator and reference-class audit."

#fig-prototype-probability fig-alt="Two paths are contrasted. The representativeness heuristic produces an impression from similarity; a probability update combines the prior probability with how likely the evidence is under the competing explanations." .phone-fit
#fig-belief-protection-loop fig-alt="Selective search, interpretation, memory, and confidence form a reinforcing loop, with disconfirming tests and independent standards as interventions."

#fig-anchor-decoy fig-alt="The anchoring panel separates the observed shift toward an available number from four possible mechanisms: insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility, scale use, and conversational inference. The attraction-effect panel shows options A and B, then an inferior decoy B-minus, and states that adding the decoy can increase B's choice share."

#fig-subscription-decoy fig-alt="Two side-by-side subscription menus show reported choices in classroom groups of 100. With a print-only decoy priced at 125 dollars, 16 chose web only at 59 dollars, none chose print only at 125 dollars, and 84 chose print plus web at 125 dollars. Without the decoy, 68 chose web only and 32 chose print plus web."

#fig-assumed-choice-eggs fig-alt="Two side-by-side menu panels. The first asks whether the person wants an egg and displays no and yes. The second asks whether the person wants one or two eggs and displays only one and two. The second question makes adding an egg implicit." width=100%

#fig-wording-memory-study-redraw fig-alt="A two-panel original chart. In Experiment 1, with 45 students in five groups of nine, mean speed estimates rise from 31.8 miles per hour for contacted to 40.8 for smashed. In Experiment 2, with 50 students per group, 32 percent of the smashed group reported broken glass versus 14 percent of the hit group and 12 percent of controls, although no broken glass appeared."
#fig-priming-pathway fig-alt="An earlier cue makes a meaning easier to retrieve. The accessible meaning and the current input converge on interpretation."

#fig-fluency-pathway fig-alt="Four possible sources—repetition, clarity, familiarity, and pronounceability—converge on processing ease. Ease can influence perceived truth, liking, confidence, or context-specific risk and safety judgment. A separate evidence check asks what caused the ease and what independent evidence supports the inference." .phone-fit

#fig-probability-judgment-map fig-alt="A natural-frequency tree starts with 10,000 people: 100 have the disease and 9,900 do not. With ninety-percent sensitivity, 90 people with disease test positive. With a nine-percent false-positive rate, 891 people without disease test positive. Therefore 90 of the 981 positive tests, about 9.2 percent, come from people with disease." width=100%

#fig-regression-conditional-shrinkage fig-alt="A fixed-seed simulation of 50 standardized measurement pairs has an approximately 0.40 sample correlation under a declared normal data-generating process. The conditional prediction line is flatter than the no-noise identity line. Guides show that an initial value two standard deviations above average predicts a second value 0.8 standard deviations above average." width=100%

#fig-confidence-accuracy fig-alt="Across four information stages, mean confidence is 33.2, 39.2, 46.0, and 52.8 percent; mean accuracy is 26.0, 23.0, 28.4, and 27.8 percent. Distinct lines and markers distinguish confidence from accuracy." .phone-fit

#fig-monty-hall-protocol fig-alt="Three stages show a Monty Hall problem. First, the chosen door receives one-third probability and the two unchosen doors receive two-thirds together. Second, a knowledgeable host opens an unchosen goat door under a constrained rule, choosing randomly when either goat door could be opened. Third, keeping retains one-third while switching receives two-thirds." width=100%

#fig-risky-decision-map fig-alt="Two-panel diagram. The left panel plots a concave square-root utility curve from wealth zero to one hundred, marks lottery outcomes zero and one hundred, shows expected value fifty, expected utility five, certainty equivalent twenty-five, and risk premium twenty-five. The right panel contrasts a transparent known-risk urn with an ambiguous urn, then shows a process arrow leading to multiple possible outcomes to emphasize that a good decision can lose and a poor decision can win." width=100%

#fig-prospect-theory-map fig-alt="Three-part diagram. The left panel shows a value function centered at a reference point: concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses. The right panel shows an inverse-S probability-weighting curve relative to the forty-five-degree objective-probability line, emphasizing possibility and certainty. The bottom panel is a four-cell table mapping high- and low-probability gains and losses to typical risk attitudes and examples." width=100%

#fig-decision-experience-states fig-alt="A two-by-two matrix. Columns indicate description absent or present; rows indicate experience absent or present. Neither is labeled information-poor. Description only means an explicit model without personal feedback; experience only means a sampled path without an explicit distribution; both means evidence sources can reinforce or conflict."

#fig-experience-rare-event-sampling fig-alt="Line chart showing the probability that a rare event has not appeared after up to one hundred independent observations. The one-percent-event curve falls slowly and the five-percent-event curve falls more quickly. A band marks sample sizes eleven to nineteen. A side panel reports that at fifteen observations a one-percent event is absent with probability eighty-six percent and a five-percent event is absent with probability forty-six percent." width=100%

#fig-mental-accounting-map fig-alt="An outcome enters a box of possible mental-accounting operations: label or open an account, code or post an outcome, bracket outcomes, and couple consumption with payment or close an account. A valuation layer compares the representation with a reference point. Two arrows show that a boundary may support a goal or distort substitution."

#fig-mental-accounting-evidence-redraw fig-alt="Two-panel comparison. The left panel contrasts a winner sold with a loser held and reports a 3.41-percentage-point difference in subsequent market-adjusted return, with a forward-looking question asking whether the investor would buy the position today. The right panel shows median hypothetical stock allocations of forty percent under annual return distributions and ninety percent under thirty-year distributions, with twenty-five participants in each group." width=100%

#fig-discount-model-crossover fig-alt="A plot compares exponential, hyperbolic, and quasi-hyperbolic discount functions with declared parameters. Below it, a worked quasi-hyperbolic example prefers 120 euros in thirteen months when both rewards are delayed but reverses to 100 euros when the smaller reward becomes immediate. A note says the exponential example remains time consistent." width=100%

#fig-intertemporal-choice fig-alt="An author's diagnostic synthesis shows two paths from a choice point. Possible bottlenecks on a delayed path include uncertainty, weak future imagery, and friction; design levers can be tested against them."

#fig-hidden-zero-frame fig-alt="Two panels show the same intertemporal payoffs. The abbreviated panel displays 100 euros today or 120 euros in one month and leaves the other dates unstated. #fig-habit-loop fig-alt="Four equal segments form a ring: Cue, Impulse, Action, and Outcome. Three solid clockwise arrows trace an episode in that order. A dashed arrow from Outcome to Cue marks a later encounter with the cue. Learning across repetitions appears in the center." .phone-fit

#fig-habit-formation-curve fig-alt="An automaticity curve crosses a horizontal dashed habit line at 95% of the plateau, labeled on the right. A vertical dotted line runs from the crossing to the time axis." width=100% fig-align="center" style="max-width: 560px !important;" .phone-fit

#fig-reward-prediction-error-shift fig-alt="Four panels show schematic changes in dopamine-neuron firing over time. A stays at baseline after a cue that does not yet predict reward, then rises at the unexpected reward. B rises at the learned cue and shows little additional response at reward. C rises at the cue and falls below baseline when reward is omitted. D rises at the cue, dips when reward was due, and rises again when the delayed reward arrives. Baseline does not mean no dopamine." .phone-fit width=98%

#fig-reward-uncertainty-comparison fig-alt="A solid teal line represents certain reward; a dashed blue line represents a 50% reward probability before the outcome. The certain cue elicits a larger brief response, followed by activity near baseline. The uncertain condition includes a smaller cue response and sustained activity increasing toward the outcome. At the outcome, a green dashed branch rises if reward is received, while a red dashed branch falls if it is omitted. Both branches share the same pre-outcome path. Curves show schematic changes in firing around baseline, not absolute dopamine release." .phone-fit width=98%

#fig-urge-wave-observation fig-alt="A schematic curve of urge intensity rises to a rounded peak and then gradually declines. The line changes from yellow through orange to red around the peak, then through purple and blue to green as intensity declines. The axes have no numerical scale." width=100% .phone-fit

#fig-well-being-six-lenses fig-alt="Four stations follow a choice through time: predicted utility before the choice, decision utility when choosing, experienced utility during the outcome, and remembered utility afterward. Each has a short guiding question. A separate band across the bottom contains life evaluation and meaning and purpose, representing broader perspectives rather than a final stage."

#fig-income-wellbeing-evidence-synthesis fig-alt="A shared legend identifies solid blue lines as life evaluation and dashed orange lines as emotional well-being across three schematic panels, all plotted against log annual household income. Kahneman and Deaton (2010): life evaluation rises while emotional well-being flattens. Killingsworth (2021): emotional well-being continues rising. Killingsworth et al. (2023): smaller annotations distinguish the least happy respondents, whose emotional well-being flattens, from happier respondents, whose emotional well-being continues rising." width=100%

#fig-level-k-reasoning-ladder fig-alt="An illustrative ladder starts from an expected random-choice anchor of fifty, then gives approximately thirty-three, twenty-two, fifteen, and the equilibrium zero for a two-thirds-of-the-mean guessing game." width=100%
